items.title: Uhuru's former top bodyguard lands new job in fresh police changes
items.description: Pepita Ranka, who led the Presidential Escort during Mr Kenyatta's presidency, has been promoted.
content: Senior Assistant Inspector-General Pepita Ranka.

A senior police officer who headed the Presidential Escort under former President Uhuru Kenyatta has been given a top posting at police headquarters, even as changes are made to an elite Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) unit that has been under public scrutiny.

Senior Assistant Inspector-General Pepita Ranka, who led the Presidential Escort during Mr Kenyatta's presidency, has been promoted from regional police commander to Director of Logistics at Vigilance House, the police headquarters.
He takes over from Peter Ndung'u, who retired from the police on November 13, 2026.

Deputy Inspector-General Eliud Lagat, who spoke at a farewell party for Mr Ndung'u at the Police Grounds in South C, praised him for his leadership, professionalism and contribution to strengthening logistical support for policing operations.
Director of Criminal Investigations (DCI) Mohammed Amin.
At the DCI, director Mohammed Amin has made changes to the Operations Support Unit (OSU).

He has appointed David Chebii as the unit's deputy head. Mr Chebii has been the Tana River County DCI boss and previously headed the Parklands-based Anti-Counterfeit unit, which was disbanded when President William Ruto took office.

Mr Amin has also directed that all of the unit's operations move to DCI headquarters on Kiambu Road. The unit is currently based at the Old Nairobi area offices, which also serve as the Nairobi County Traffic Headquarters. The move appears aimed at rebranding and reorganising the unit.
The current head of the OSU, Zachary Kariuki, is serving on contract after reaching the mandatory retirement age of 60.

Mr Amin created the OSU after President Ruto ordered the disbandment of a former police unit, the Special Crimes Prevention Unit (SCPU), following accusations that its members were involved in criminal activities.

On September 13, 2022, soon after taking office, Dr Ruto promised that his administration would not entertain secret police units such as the DCI Special Service Unit. He said the police would operate independently and would not be used to harass people with divergent views.

The SCPU was linked to the disappearance and killing of two Indian nationals who were part of Mr Ruto's presidential campaign team, and of a taxi driver who was driving them when they were abducted in Nairobi.

Mohammed Zaid Sami Kidwai, Zulfiqra Ahmed Khan and Nichodemus Mwania Mwange went missing on July 23, 2022. The two Indians were part of a five-man team that arrived in the country as tourists on April 16 and visited several places in the Rift Valley and Nairobi.
Mohamed Zaid Sami and Zulfiqar Ahmed Khan who were killed between July 22 and 23, 2022.

Police investigations led by Mr Amin, who was then head of the Police Internal Affairs Unit, and CCTV footage placed at least 28 DCI officers from the Special Service Unit at the centre of the abduction and disappearance of the three men.

"I have directed that immediate measures be undertaken to disband the Special Services Unit in the DCI and with urgency investigations must commence so that those found culpable are held accountable," President Ruto said in his Mashujaa Day speech.
After the SCPU was disbanded, Mr Amin created the OSU. The unit's focus came under sharp scrutiny at the height of the 2024 anti-Finance Bill protests.
It has been scrutinised further after some of its members were accused of abductions, including the attack on Standard Group editor Alex Kiprotich.

On July 9, former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua claimed at a press conference in Nairobi that he knew of a secret police unit attached to the National Intelligence Service (NIS) that was responsible for the abduction and killing of peaceful protesters. He claimed that the covert unit was assembled while he was still in government and was highly trained for covert operations.

The government has denied that any police squad is involved in extrajudicial killings. Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen has said that all police operations are conducted in accordance with the law.
"In the event any police officer is accused of unlawful use of force, they will face the law," he said.

items.title: Kenya and Switzerland deepen bilateral climate partnership at COP 31
items.description: Kenya and Switzerland deepen bilateral climate partnership at COP 31 Kenya News Agency Kenya and Switzerland authorise first Article 6.2 carbon programme for 226,000 Roam electric motorcycles THE PACK – Electric motorcycle news Cabinet Secretary (CS) for Environment, Climate Change and Forestry, Dr. Deborah Barasa (Right) poses for a photo with the landmark Kenya–Switzerland Article 6 Implementing Agreement during high-level bilateral engagements at the Swiss Delegation Offi Facebook Swiss approve 1st project under Kenyan Art. 6 deal for 1.7m ITMOs Quantum Commodity Intelligence
content: Environment, Climate Change and Forestry Cabinet Secretary, Dr. Deborah Barasa has reaffirmed Kenya’s commitment to operationalizing the landmark Kenya–Switzerland Article 6 Implementing Agreement during high-level bilateral engagements at the Swiss Delegation Office on the sidelines of COP 31.

Following the Agreement’s signing in Bern in May 2025 and its entry into force in June 2026, both nations are moving decisively from policy to implementation to unlock high-integrity carbon markets that drive climate action and economic growth.

This strategic partnership is projected to deliver 5 million tonnes of CO₂ equivalent in mitigation outcomes while mobilizing USD 520 million in direct investments, generating USD 200 million in carbon revenues alongside USD 21.2 million in Designated National Authority (DNA) fees, and creating approximately 115,000 green jobs.
Further, momentum on the ground is already building, with eight projects registered across electric mobility, biogas, solar water pumping, and clean cooking.

Notably, four of these initiatives have already received Letters of Approval from Kenya’s DNA, including the recent issuance of a revised Letter of Approval for Roam Electric in October 2026, underscoring the Government’s commitment to facilitating implementation within its existing legal framework.

During the engagements, Dr. Barasa emphasized regulatory predictability and investor confidence, pointing to the Government’s formal communication to Switzerland on 6 th , November 2026 that confirmed Kenya’s authorization pathway.

“Under the Climate Change Act (Cap. 387A) and the Carbon Markets Regulations, 2024, Kenya remains committed to authorizing eligible projects, applying corresponding adjustments, and recognizing the international transfer and use of verified Internationally Transferred Mitigation Outcomes (ITMOs),” the CS reaffirmed.

Furthermore, she noted that the mitigation volumes for activities with Letters of Approval have already been factored into Kenya’s carbon budget under the Kenya Guide for Strategic Engagement in Carbon Markets (2026).

While both countries issue their own independent authorizations under their respective domestic laws, Kenya has proposed establishing a Joint Technical Working Group—bringing together representatives from Switzerland, NEMA, the Climate Change Directorate, and the Ministry’s Legal Unit, to swiftly address any emerging technical or regulatory challenges.

Alongside this, Dr. Barasa called for expedited Swiss reviews and authorizations for projects that have already fulfilled Kenya’s domestic regulatory requirements to fast-track financial closure and investment mobilization.

Meanwhile, the Ministry remains steadfast in working closely with Switzerland to champion transparent, high-integrity carbon markets that deliver tangible climate resilience, green investments, and sustainable development for all Kenyans.

items.title: 27 years on, family seeks justice over alleged police killing
items.description: Dominic Musomba died in a violent shoot-out in Nairobi. His grandchildren want Ipoa to reopen...
content: Dominic Kioko, grandson of the late Dominic Musomba Wambua, during an interview on November 22, 2026, in which he called for investigations into his grandfather's death in a 1999 police shoot-out to be reopened.
Twenty-seven years after Dominic Musomba Wambua was killed in a violent shoot-out, the pain of losing him has not faded, nor has his family's quest for answers.

What began as an apparently ordinary Saturday morning on April 24, 1999, ended in tragedy when Wambua, then 38, was caught up in an exchange of gunfire between police and suspected bank robbers shortly after arriving in Nairobi's city centre to run personal errands.

His death not only cut short his life but also disrupted the future of his five children, who lost their sole breadwinner. The effects of the loss have since extended to another generation, with his grandchildren growing up without knowing him.
Dominic Kioko, grandson of the late Dominic Musomba Wambua, called for investigations into his grandfather's death in a 1999 police shoot-out to be reopened.

Now, a new generation is determined to keep the family's quest alive. His grandson, Dominic Kioko, wants the circumstances surrounding his grandfather's death investigated and those responsible held to account.
“We, the grandchildren, have lived knowing that our grandfather was innocently killed at the hands of the police,” says Kioko, 21.

He was not yet born when the incident happened but says that has not diminished his determination to pursue the matter. The family is now seeking the intervention of the Independent Policing Oversight Authority (Ipoa) to reopen investigations and establish what happened.
Kioko says previous attempts to seek redress through government institutions have yielded little.

“Despite the years that have passed, our wounds are still fresh. I have visited the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR), but I have not received the help we need. No one was arrested, the government has never explained what happened, and our demand for an inquest has gone unanswered,” he says.
Beyond the loss of their grandfather, Kioko says the family continues to grapple with the economic consequences of his death, particularly the disruption of his children's education and livelihoods.
“His children did not get the education they should have because his life was cut short. We have never received compensation or even an official communication from the government,” he says.
He is also troubled by the circumstances surrounding Wambua's death, particularly an additional bullet wound he says was discovered on the body.

“It is very sad that people entrusted with protecting lives could be responsible for someone's death. Where did the additional bullet come from? We need to know what happened after he was shot,” he says.

In pursuit of redress, Kioko approached KNCHR and was advised to submit a claim to the Panel of Experts on Compensation of Victims of Human Rights Violations, including those arising from demonstrations and public protests. He says the panel provided a claim form, which he completed and returned.
Documents seen by the Nation show that Kioko submitted the claim as Wambua's representative, with authorisation from his widow, Rose Nduku.

The claim identifies officers from the Kenya Police Flying Squad and Quick Response Mobile Unit as responsible for the killing. It lists the harm suffered as death, torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, loss of livelihood, economic loss and psychological trauma.

In his account, Kioko states that Wambua was shot in the chest but remained alive when placed at the back of a police Land Cruiser. He alleges that his grandfather died while in police custody on the way to hospital.
He further states that the body was taken to City Mortuary, now Nairobi Funeral Home, with an additional bullet wound to the mouth or head.

The claim describes Wambua as the family's sole breadwinner, saying his death deprived his widow and children of income, school fees and basic support. It also states that Nduku and the children have continued to suffer psychological trauma, while their education and upkeep were adversely affected.
In a letter dated September 29, 2026, addressed to the KNCHR chairperson, Kioko formally sought intervention over what he describes as his grandfather's extrajudicial killing.

He refers to the incident involving the Housing Finance Company of Kenya (HFCK), now HF, Gill House branch robbery, which was reported by the Daily Nation and documented by the Kenya Human Rights Commission (KHRC).
According to the letter, KHRC had previously urged the Commissioner of Police to investigate the killing, take action against those responsible and ensure the family was compensated.
Read: Two killed, others injured in suspected gas explosion at KPA cafeteria
Kioko further alleges that the police file disappeared at Vigilance House, no inquest was conducted, no officer was charged and the family received no compensation.

He is asking KNCHR to help reopen the file, provide the family with a copy of the commission's earlier correspondence to the Attorney-General and assist in tracing police records, including the Occurrence Book (OB) number. He has also requested assistance in securing pro bono legal representation to pursue a High Court petition.
“The worst part of this case is not merely the loss of life but the absence of justice. I refuse to allow 26 years of unanswered questions to be met with silence,” he says.

On the fateful day, April 24, 1999, Wambua had left his colleagues at Nairobi Bottling Company in Industrial Area at about 8.30am on, intending to travel to his rural home in Kibwezi after running personal errands in town.
About half an hour later, suspected robbers raided the HFCK Gill House branch and escaped with Sh3.5 million, triggering a shoot-out with police officers.

The robbery began shortly after 9.00am when two armed men, posing as customers, entered the banking hall, confronted a cashier and ordered everyone to lie down before taking the money. Officers from the Flying Squad and Quick Response Mobile Unit arrived shortly afterwards, prompting an exchange of gunfire.

During the confrontation, one of the robbers was shot and wounded but was pulled back to his feet by a colleague who fired at the officers as they dragged him towards a getaway vehicle. The gang sped towards the nearby Kenya Railways station as the gunfight continued.

Wambua was reportedly hit by a bullet during the second exchange of fire. Newspaper accounts at the time quoted witnesses as saying he was shot in the chest near the bank entrance, staggered onto the pavement and lay writhing in pain before police officers placed him in the back of their Land Rover.
His photograph, showing him seated in the vehicle with his jacket soaked in blood, appeared in newspapers the following day.

His brother, Wambua Musyoki, and colleagues recognised him in the photograph and began searching police stations and hospitals. Their search ended at City Mortuary, where they found his body bearing an additional gunshot wound to the mouth that had shattered his brain.
The discovery raised questions about when and how he sustained the fatal injury, given that witnesses had reportedly seen him alive after being shot in the chest and placed in the police vehicle.

Police, however, maintained that Wambua was among six gang members involved in the robbery. The account was disputed by witnesses, including bank guard Ronald Simiyu, who said he saw only two armed men enter the premises, while others may have been waiting outside in the getaway vehicle.
The conflicting accounts of his involvement in the robbery and the circumstances surrounding his death remain central to the family's demand for an explanation.

Treasury targets Sh1.23tn borrowing to finance Sh5.2tn budget
items.description: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 23 – The National Treasury plans to borrow Sh1.23 trillion to finance the proposed Sh5.24 trillion national budget for the 2027/28 financial year, highlighting the government’s continued…
content: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 23 – The National Treasury plans to borrow Sh1.23 trillion to finance the proposed Sh5.24 trillion national budget for the 2027/28 financial year, highlighting the government’s continued reliance on debt to meet its spending commitments.

Treasury Principal Secretary Chris Kiptoo says the government expects to collect Sh3.92 trillion in revenue during the financial year starting July 2027, leaving a financing gap equivalent to 5.4 percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
The deficit will be financed through net domestic borrowing of Sh658.9 billion and external borrowing of Sh570 billion.
The borrowing plan comes amid revenue collection challenges, with the government missing its revenue targets in the first quarter of the current 2026/27 financial year.

By the end of September 2026, total government revenue, including Appropriations in Aid (A-i-A), stood at Sh801.5 billion against a target of Sh859.9 billion, representing a shortfall of Sh58.4 billion.

items.title: Sifuna warns opposition: deliver change in 90 days or face the streets
items.description: Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna has warned that an opposition government replacing Ruto in 2027 must deliver change within 90 days or face renewed street protests from Kenyans.
content: The Nairobi senator tells Kenyans in the United States that a post-Ruto government will have no grace period — and that the Linda Mwananchi movement will hold any successor to the same standard it holds the current administration.

Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna has warned that an opposition government replacing President William Ruto after the 2027 General Election would have no more than three months to demonstrate meaningful change before Kenyans returned to the streets, setting one of the starkest accountability benchmarks yet articulated by a senior figure in the emerging opposition coalition.

Sifuna delivered the warning during engagements with Kenyans living in the United States, where he has been meeting diaspora communities as part of efforts to build momentum for the Linda Mwananchi movement ahead of next year’s election. His message was directed as much at his own political allies as at the electorate — a deliberate signal that opposition unity, should it materialise, would carry obligations that did not expire at the ballot box.

“If we slacken, if we go there and continue with business as usual, it will not take more than three months — these young people will be back in the street saying, ‘The government must go,'” Sifuna said, referencing the Gen Z-led protests that convulsed Kenya in June 2024 and forced Ruto to withdraw the Finance Bill under sustained public pressure.

The reference was pointed and entirely intentional. Those protests — which drew tens of thousands of young Kenyans into the streets of Nairobi, Mombasa, Kisumu and beyond, resulted in approximately 62 deaths according to human rights organisations, and briefly breached the perimeter of Parliament Buildings — fundamentally altered the political landscape of Ruto’s presidency. They demonstrated, with a clarity that no opinion poll could match, that Kenya’s youth were prepared to hold governments to account through direct action when they felt that constitutional and electoral processes had failed them. Sifuna was telling his audience, and through them the opposition leadership, that the generation which brought down the Finance Bill would apply exactly the same standard to whoever succeeded Ruto.

It is a position that sets Sifuna apart from much of the opposition discourse currently circulating in Kenya’s political arena, where the conversation has concentrated heavily on the mechanics of defeating Ruto rather than on what victory would actually require in its immediate aftermath. While former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua builds his Democracy for the Citizens Party network across the Mt Kenya region, and while various opposition figures jockey for positioning within potential coalition arrangements, Sifuna is insisting that the more urgent question is what a post-Ruto administration would do in its first quarter — and whether opposition leaders have agreed on the answer before asking Kenyans to trust them with power.

His conditions for unity are specific and economically focused. Sifuna said opposition leaders must, before forming a united political front, reach consensus on immediate measures to ease the financial burden on ordinary households. He cited reducing or eliminating taxes on fuel and electricity, and scrapping the housing levy — a mandatory deduction from payrolls that has been among the most bitterly contested elements of the Ruto administration’s fiscal policy — as priorities that any credible opposition platform must commit to delivering promptly after a change of government.

“We are not going to government to get comfortable. There will be no room for being comfortable,” Sifuna said, in remarks that carried an implicit rebuke of political cultures in which opposition movements, having secured power, rapidly accommodated themselves to the same patronage structures and spending habits they had campaigned against.

The senator argued that reducing government expenditure to create fiscal space for tax relief was not merely a policy preference but a precondition for public trust. Kenyans had, in his reading, reached a point of acute impatience with administrations that promised relief and delivered rationalisation. An opposition government that arrived in office and then began explaining why the promised changes were more complicated than anticipated would, he suggested, face a public that had heard the explanation before and was no longer prepared to accept it.

The political context surrounding Sifuna’s US trip extends beyond his remarks on accountability timelines. His engagements drew attention to a proposal, raised during a meeting with diaspora members on Saturday, that Kenyans living abroad could mobilise resources to support the construction of Jomo Kenyatta International Airport. Participant Kiemo Mohando put the idea directly: “We can build the airport. Don’t look for another Adani. We can build an airport. We can reorganise ourselves — let’s partner with the government, let’s do the airport.”

The reference to Adani placed Mohando’s proposal in an immediate and politically charged context. India’s Adani Group has featured prominently in debates about Kenya’s aviation infrastructure, and the broader controversy surrounding the conglomerate’s international operations — including bribery allegations in the United States — has made any association with Adani infrastructure projects politically sensitive in Kenya. Mohando’s suggestion that the diaspora could serve as an alternative financing source for JKIA tapped into a genuine appetite within Kenyan communities abroad to participate more directly in national development. It remained, however, a participant’s proposal rather than a formal commitment by any organised diaspora body, and Sifuna’s office did not indicate that it had been formally adopted as opposition policy.

What the exchange did illuminate is the degree to which Kenyans outside the country are engaging with the pre-election political debate with an intensity that rival the conversations happening in Nairobi’s political circles. The diaspora — concentrated in the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada and the Gulf — represents not only a source of remittances that constitute a significant portion of Kenya’s foreign exchange earnings, but an increasingly vocal constituency that opposition and government figures alike are competing to address.

For Sifuna, the US engagements served a dual purpose: reinforcing the Linda Mwananchi movement’s national reach and testing the resonance of a message built on accountability rather than simply on anti-Ruto sentiment. The distinction matters. Kenya has cycled through enough post-election disappointments to have produced a cohort of voters, particularly among the young, who are as sceptical of opposition promises as they are of government performance.

Telling that cohort that a new government would face the streets within 90 days of failing to deliver is either a remarkable act of political honesty or a carefully calibrated piece of positioning — perhaps both simultaneously. In Kenya’s pre-election landscape, the two are not always easy to distinguish.

What is clear is that the standard Sifuna has articulated publicly now follows the opposition into every conversation it has between now and August 2027. He has set the clock. The question is whether his allies are prepared to run against it.

items.title: Karua, Matiang’i and Nyoro take opposition message to Kirinyaga
items.description: Martha Karua, Fred Matiang'i and Ndindi Nyoro rallied Kirinyaga County residents in Kutus and Ngarubaini under the TuunganeTujikomboe banner ahead of Kenya's 2027 elections.
content: Karua, Matiang’i and Nyoro take opposition message to Kirinyaga
The Kutus rally signals a sharpening alliance as Kenya’s emerging opposition bloc tests its reach in Mt Kenya heartland.

Martha Karua, former Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i and Kiharu Member of Parliament Ndindi Nyoro on Sunday took their opposition campaign to Kirinyaga County, addressing residents in Kutus and Ngarubaini in what organisers described as an overwhelmingly attended series of public engagements under the #TuunganeTujikomboe banner.

Karua, speaking after the rally, framed the gathering in deliberately measured terms, pushing back against suggestions that the emerging alliance represented political opportunism. “Democracy is built on dialogue, engagement and the willingness to find common ground,” she said. “Political alliances and partnerships are part of that process, and there is no need to mistake discussion for division.”

The trio’s appearance together in Kirinyaga — a county that sits squarely within the Mt Kenya region whose political loyalty is now fiercely contested ahead of the 2027 General Election — carries significance beyond the warm receptions reported at both venues. It represents a visible effort to plant an opposition flag in territory that President William Ruto carried convincingly in 2022.

Karua was direct about the coalition’s intended focus. “Our attention must remain firmly on the people,” she said. “Kenyans want relief from the rising cost of living, opportunities for employment, better education and accessible healthcare. They want to live with dignity and have reason to believe in tomorrow.”
The road to 2027 runs through Mt Kenya. Yesterday, three of its most prominent voices served notice they intend to contest every inch of it.

items.description: Nairobi hosted the grand finale of Africa’s Next Super Model 2026 at Broadwalk Mall on Saturday, 21 November, with the competition endorsed by the Ministry of Tourism and Wildlife. Model…
content: Nairobi hosted the grand finale of Africa’s Next Super Model 2026 at Broadwalk Mall on Saturday, 21 November, with the competition endorsed by the Ministry of Tourism and Wildlife. Model Nyaliep Puot was crowned winner, beating 19 other contestants from across the continent. She won a $5,000 prize, global exposure and the chance to work with luxury international fashion brands.

The finale opened with the Kenyan National Anthem and remarks from founder Joan Okorodudu, CEO of Isis Models International. She thanked the Government of Kenya for endorsing and supporting the competition. The Ministry’s endorsement shows that the government values the platform’s role in nurturing talent and lifting the creative economy.
Nyandech Changath was named first runner-up and Nyayiel James second runner-up. Nyaliep follows Dillah Acelle, who won the title in 2025.

Judges singled out the new champion’s confidence, poise and professionalism. “She showed immense confidence. She is destined for great stages,” said judge Matteo Puglisi, CEO of Select Models Management. He said the competition is opening international doors for African models and connecting them to global brands, which he described as life- changing.

For Nyaliep, the win was emotional. “I can’t believe it. It wasn’t an easy journey, so winning is fulfilling. I thank everyone who supported me in this and congratulate all the other finalists,” she said.

Kenyan court declines to block Dangote’s 24.76% stake in pipeline company
items.description: Kenya’s High Court has declined to suspend transactions involving Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote’s 24.76 percent stake in Kenya...
content: Kenya’s High Court has declined to suspend transactions involving Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote’s 24.76 percent stake in Kenya Pipeline Company (KPC), leaving a legal challenge over the sale of shares by public institutions unresolved ahead of the company’s December 2 annual general meeting. Advertisement Advertisement Justice Patricia Nyaundi Mande, in directions issued on November 10, declined to certify the application as urgent or grant interim orders before hearing the other parties in a petition filed by human rights activist Francis Awino. “This is not an appropriate matter for the grant of ex parte orders,” the court stated. Read also: Dangote set for Kenya Pipeline board seat after acquiring 24.9% stake The judge directed the respondents to file their replies by November 27, with the matter scheduled for mention on November 30, two days before KPC’s annual general meeting. The decision leaves the requested interim restrictions unenforced but does not resolve the substantive allegations or establish whether the transactions complied with applicable laws and regulations. Advertisement Dangote’s investment vehicle is expected to continue preparations to nominate a director ahead of the shareholder meeting, a move that could result in the National Social Security Fund (NSSF) losing its representation on KPC’s board. The petition, filed by Awino, challenges the acquisition, holding and disposal of shares in KPC by public institutions and pension funds, seeking greater disclosure of the decisions and approvals behind the transactions. Advertisement The activist is asking the court to compel the institutions involved to provide details of the shares transferred, transaction dates, proceeds received, approvals obtained and the processes used to execute the deals. The requested documents include investment appraisals, board and trustee resolutions, fund-manager instructions, transaction agreements and payment records. Institutions identified in reports by Business Daily and The Star include the NSSF, Public Service Superannuation Fund, County Pension Fund, Lapfund and Laptrust, alongside pension schemes linked to Kenya Power, KPC and Kenya Ports Authority. Advertisement Advertisement The respondents include the National Treasury, Privatisation Authority, Capital Markets Authority, KPC, pension institutions and a Dangote-linked refinery company. At the heart of the dispute is whether the public institutions involved followed the required procedures in acquiring, holding and disposing of their shares in the pipeline company, and how proceeds from the transactions were accounted for. Read also: Dangote stake makes Kenya Pipeline fourth most valuable firm on NSE The court has not made any findings of wrongdoing against the institutions or parties involved, with the petition still awaiting substantive determination. Dangote’s investment in KPC Dangote acquired approximately 24.76 percent of KPC in October 2026 in a deal valued at about $327 million, giving his investment group a significant stake in infrastructure that connects Kenya’s coastal petroleum facilities to inland and regional markets. The acquisition forms part of his broader expansion into East Africa’s energy sector. KPC plays a central role in petroleum transportation and distribution in Kenya, making its ownership and governance structure significant to the region’s energy supply network. The pending petition seeks to scrutinise the public-sector shareholding arrangements that preceded the acquisition and the institutional decisions behind the transfer of the shares. Dangote’s broader energy plans in Kenya have also faced scrutiny over a separate proposed $16 billion refinery project in Lamu. In October, a Kenyan court lifted an earlier restriction on the project, allowing development to proceed while the legal dispute continued. Separately, a consumer group has sought details of Kenya’s proposed $500 million investment in the refinery following plans for East African governments to participate in the project. Read also: Dangote plans $1.5bn expansion of Kenya Pipeline network The refinery-related proceedings and investment questions are distinct from the KPC shareholding petition, which focuses on transactions involving shares in the pipeline company by public institutions and pension funds. The KPC case is expected to return to court on November 30, following the deadline for respondents to file their replies on November 27. The hearing schedule comes just ahead of the December 2 shareholder meeting. For now, the court’s refusal to grant immediate restrictions leaves preparations for the meeting in place, while the legality of the share transactions and the allegations raised by the petitioner remain unresolved. The Kenya Meteorological Service Authority (KMSA) has released its weekly weather outlook for the period spanning November 24 to 30, 2026, projecting continued rainfall across 30 counties alongside sharply contrasting temperature extremes between the country's highlands and arid north.
KMSA published the forecast on Monday, November 23, 2026, via WhatsApp.
The authority indicated that wet conditions are set to persist across a wide swathe of the country.

Counties expected to receive rainfall include Kakamega, Bungoma, Nandi, Homa Bay, Migori, Kisii, Kericho, Nyamira, Nyandarua, Laikipia, Nyeri, Murang'a, Kiambu, Nairobi, Kirinyaga, Embu, Tharaka Nithi, Meru, Isiolo, Kitui, Makueni, Machakos, Kajiado, Taita Taveta, Tana River, Garissa, Lamu, Kilifi, Kwale, and Mombasa.
The list spans the western highlands, the Mount Kenya region, Nairobi, and much of the Coast, suggesting the long rains season is maintaining its reach across a large portion of the 47 counties.

Residents in highland areas face notably cold nights during the forecast window. Minimum temperatures below 10°C are expected in parts of Meru, Tharaka Nithi, Nyeri, Kirinyaga, Murang'a, Nyandarua, Laikipia, Nakuru , Elgeyo Marakwet, Trans Nzoia, Taita Taveta, and Kajiado Counties.
At the other extreme, the country's arid and semi-arid northern and coastal zones are forecast to record daytime highs exceeding 35°C.
Parts of Samburu, Turkana, Marsabit, Wajir, Garissa, and Lamu counties are expected to bear the brunt of intense afternoon heat through the week.

The divergence underscores Kenya's wide climatic range, where temperatures across the country can differ by more than 25°C on the same day depending on elevation and geography.
KMSA urged the public to stay informed and prepared ahead of the week's conditions.
Meanwhile, farmers in Limuru and Karatina are using sandbags, trenches, Napier grass , and bamboo to protect their land from forecast El Niño rains.
After losing crops and fertile topsoil in the 2024 floods, farmers are turning to low-cost methods to limit damage.
The floods killed more than 230 people, and forecasters expect November to bring peak rainfall in several parts of the country.

items.title: John Korir withdraws from Valencia Marathon defence through injury
items.description: The Mount Kenya Times Kenya’s Boston champion will miss the 6 December race, but a formidable squad still lines up for the City of Running.Thank you for reading this post, don't forget to subscribe! By Martin Weche John Korir, Kenya’s reigning Valencia Marathon champion, has withdrawn from this year’s edition of the race through injury, […]
content: Kenya’s Boston champion will miss the 6 December race, but a formidable squad still lines up for the City of Running.

John Korir, Kenya’s reigning Valencia Marathon champion, has withdrawn from this year’s edition of the race through injury, ending his bid to defend the title he claimed in the Spanish city twelve months ago.

Race organisers confirmed the news in an official statement, citing an injury sustained during Korir’s preparation for the 6 December event. “Unfortunately, the current Valencia Marathon winner, John Korir, will not be able to defend his title in 2026,” the statement read. “The Kenyan star has decided to withdraw from the race due to injury. We wish John a speedy recovery and hope to welcome him back to the City of Running very soon.”

The withdrawal is a significant blow, both personally and competitively. Korir, 29, had arrived at this point in the season in the form of his life. At the Boston Marathon in April, he clocked 2:01:52 to cross the finish line first — a performance that underlined his status as one of the most complete marathon runners in the world and placed him firmly among the favourites for another Valencia title. Earlier in the season, he had also won the senior men’s 10km at the Sirikwa Classic World Cross Country Tour in 29:44, demonstrating the depth of conditioning that makes his enforced absence all the more frustrating.

Injury has a particular cruelty in long-distance running. The sport demands months of accumulated training — controlled mileage, speed work, altitude camps, and the careful calibration of fatigue and recovery — and a single setback in the final weeks can render all of it irrelevant. For Korir, who had every reason to believe Valencia 2026 could be another landmark performance, that reality will sting deeply.

For Kenyan athletics, however, the story does not end with Korir’s withdrawal. The East African nation arrives in Valencia with one of the most formidable men’s marathon squads assembled for a single race this season, and the depth of that field ensures that Kenya’s dominance of the sport’s elite tier remains entirely intact.

Alexander Mutiso, who claimed the 2024 London Marathon title, heads a Kenyan contingent that reads less like a national entry and more like a talent identification exercise for the sport’s global hierarchy. Mutiso’s London victory demonstrated an ability to perform under pressure in one of the world’s most competitive marathon environments, and Valencia’s flat, fast course — consistently among the fastest in the world calendar — suits his strengths well.

Geoffrey Toroitich, the 2025 Amsterdam Marathon champion, adds further weight to Kenya’s challenge. Amsterdam has a reputation for producing quick times on a course that rewards efficient running, and Toroitich’s victory there suggests he has both the fitness and the tactical intelligence to compete at the front of a Valencia field. Vincent Ngetich, Samwel Mailu and Benson Tunyo complete a squad that, in almost any other year, would be considered extraordinary depth. In 2026, it is simply Kenya’s backup plan.

Valencia has earned its reputation as the City of Running through a combination of ideal December weather, a meticulously designed route and an organisational infrastructure that consistently delivers world-class conditions. The race has become a fixture for athletes chasing personal bests and national records, and the 2026 edition — with its mix of established champions and ambitious contenders — carries all the hallmarks of another exceptional day of marathon running.

The women’s race and the broader international field will add further intrigue, but it is the Kenyan men’s battle that will draw the sharpest attention on 6 December. Without Korir to defend, the question of which of his compatriots steps into the vacuum becomes the dominant narrative of the race.

Mutiso is the natural frontrunner by recent form and pedigree. But marathon running has a habit of elevating the unexpected, and in a Kenyan squad of this quality, any of the five men lining up in Valencia carries the credentials to cause a surprise.

For Korir, the focus now shifts entirely to recovery. At 29, with a Boston title and a Valencia crown already on his record, there is no urgency beyond health. Valencia will still be there next December.
Kenya, meanwhile, will not be short of champions trying to fill his shoes.

items.description: Coca-Cola has returned to African football for the first time in nearly 30 years as the official sponsor for the 2027 TotalEnergies CAF Africa Cup of Nations in Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda, as well as the 2028 edition, whose hosts are yet to be decided.
content: Coca-Cola has returned to African football for the first time in nearly 30 years as the official sponsor for the 2027 TotalEnergies CAF Africa Cup of Nations in Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda, as well as the 2028 edition, whose hosts are yet to be decided.
The agreement was signed in Johannesburg, South Africa today, Monday, 23 November 2026, by CAF President Dr. Patrice Motsepe and Luis Felipe Avellar, President of Coca-Cola’s Africa Operating Unit.

The partnership marks an exciting new chapter in Coca-Cola’s longstanding connection to African football, bringing together two icons united by a shared passion for the game and its ability to connect people across the continent.
The TotalEnergies CAF Africa Cup of Nations is Africa’s biggest sporting event, with over 3.2 billion TV audience members and 6.1 billion digital views for the 2025 edition.

CAF President Dr. Patrice Motsepe said: “CAF is excited to welcome Coca-Cola back to African football after almost 30 years, and we are confident that the partnership between CAF and Coca-Cola will contribute to the development and growth of football on the African continent and advance Coca-Cola’s commercial and stakeholder interests.

The substantial confidence that African and international sponsors, partners, and investors are showing in CAF is a recognition of the governance, ethics, transparency, and business best practices that we have introduced, as well as the world-class quality and global competitiveness of African football and CAF’s competitions.”

Luis Felipe Avellar, President of Coca-Cola’s Africa, said: “African football is a powerful source of pride, unity, and inspiration across our continent. Coca-Cola is proud to reunite with CAF and return to a tournament that holds such a special place in African football. As we look ahead to TotalEnergies CAF AFCON 2027, we are excited to celebrate the fans and communities who make the game what it is across the continent.”
Coca-Cola has been part of this history, having supported the tournament in 1996 in South Africa and 1998 in Burkina Faso.

Through its partnership with CAF, Coca-Cola will celebrate the people, cultures, and shared experiences that make African football unique, connecting the game with music, creativity, and local expression while creating opportunities for fans to experience the excitement of AFCON Pamoja 2027.

Kenya's former vice president Arthur Moody Awori is approaching a remarkable century, and his family made sure to mark the milestone in style.
Photos and videos of a heartwarming birthday gathering, shared online around November 22, quickly captured the attention of Kenyans across social media.
In the footage, Awori sat before a white birthday cake adorned with lit candles, made a wish, and blew them out as his family erupted in cheers.

Nieces, nephews and other loved ones gathered closely around him, belting out Happy Birthday in a moment that clearly moved many who watched it online.

Awori was born on December 5, 1927, meaning his official 99th birthday falls on December 5, 2026. The early celebrations, however, were more than enough to get Kenyans talking.
What struck many viewers was not just the milestone itself, but how Awori looked and carried himself throughout.
Comments flooded in praising his upright posture, sharp presence and energetic demeanour, with fans noting he walks without a walking stick.
Some joked that the former VP appeared younger than people in their thirties and sixties.

Awori served as Kenya's ninth vice president under the late President Mwai Kibaki , holding the position from September 2003 to January 2008.
He took on the role following the death of Michael Kijana Wamalwa and also served as Minister for Home Affairs during his time in government.

He is widely remembered for his calm, diplomatic style and for introducing meaningful reforms in the prison system, most notably replacing cramped metallic police trucks, commonly known as "mariamu," with buses for transporting remandees to court.
As he inches closer to 100, it is clear that Kenyans have not forgotten what he stood for.

items.title: AI is making Kenyan students faster — but are they thinking better?
items.description: AI tools are reshaping learning across Kenya's schools and TVET colleges, but educators warn the system must prioritise critical thinking over faster access to answers
content: Generative tools are reshaping classrooms from Nairobi to rural TVET colleges, but educators warn that speed without judgement is not learning.

Artificial intelligence is changing how Kenyan students learn, but the education system’s most pressing challenge is ensuring that faster access to information translates into deeper understanding rather than a sophisticated shortcut to the same shallow thinking it has always struggled to address.

From secondary schools and universities to TVET institutions and professional training programmes, learners across Kenya can now use AI tools to summarise notes, explain difficult concepts, generate essay structures and produce written work in seconds. The opportunity is real and significant. So is the risk of mistaking the speed of an answer for the quality of the thinking behind it.

The question facing Kenya’s education institutions is no longer whether students will use AI. Many already do, quietly and routinely, in ways that range from entirely legitimate to academically dishonest. What matters now is whether they are being taught to use it with judgement — and whether the system is measuring the right things.

Verification must come first. Generative AI produces confident, well-structured responses that can be incomplete, outdated or factually wrong. A student researching Kenya’s economic policy, climate record, constitutional history or public health data cannot assume that a fluent paragraph is an accurate one. Learners need to compare sources, check publication dates, interrogate claims and develop an instinct for where information originates and who benefits from its framing.

This reality makes critical thinking more valuable, not less. For much of Kenya’s education history, students were rewarded for locating and reproducing information — the right answer in the right place at the right time. In an AI-enabled learning environment, the more important skill is assessing whether information is credible, relevant and applicable to a specific problem, and then doing something useful with it. That is a harder skill to teach and a harder one to examine, but it is the one that will determine how well a graduate functions in a workplace where AI is already embedded.

Privacy requires clearer and earlier guidance than most institutions are currently providing. Students should understand that personal data, confidential school records and sensitive information should not be entered into public AI platforms without consideration of where that data goes and how it is stored. As Kenya continues to build its data protection culture under the Data Protection Act and the oversight of the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner, responsible technology use must become part of digital literacy from an early age.

The plagiarism question demands a more considered institutional response than outright prohibition. Banning AI tools is difficult to enforce, often counterproductive and can obscure the larger pedagogical point. Education should measure whether a learner understands a subject, can defend a position under questioning and can apply knowledge to unfamiliar problems. That demands a greater emphasis on oral presentations, classroom discussions, practical assignments and project-based assessments — formats in which AI assistance is visible and the student’s own thinking is unavoidable.

Prompting is itself becoming a teachable and genuinely useful skill. A learner who can frame a precise question, provide sufficient context, refine an instruction and critically evaluate the response is developing capabilities that employers across sectors are beginning to actively seek. But prompting should sharpen thinking, not replace it. The student who accepts the first output without interrogation has not learned to use AI — they have learned to defer to it.

Parents and teachers carry responsibilities that go beyond policing tool use. The more productive questions are not whether a student used AI, but how they verified the answer, what they learned in the process, what they would challenge in the output and whether they can explain the idea without the tool in front of them. Those questions shift the focus from enforcement to education, which is where it belongs.

These capabilities will matter well beyond any examination hall. As AI integrates further into Kenya’s workplaces, employers will need people who can assess AI-generated information with scepticism, identify errors, exercise independent judgement and apply knowledge to problems that do not have pre-generated answers. Using AI fluently is useful. Knowing when to question its output is essential.

Kenya’s education system has navigated significant technology transitions before — computer studies, mobile learning, digital content, online classrooms. Each demanded adaptation. Each rewarded the institutions that treated the technology as a tool in service of learning rather than a substitute for it.

AI presents the same challenge at greater speed and scale. The institutions that respond best will be those that teach students not only how to access the technology, but how to question it, use it responsibly and combine it with the one thing no model can replicate: human judgement applied to real consequences.
AI can help Kenyan learners move faster. Education must still teach them how to think.

content: Meru came alive as Kenya Cane took its 50th anniversary celebrations to Checkmate, treating revellers to an exciting night of music, entertainment and shared moments in honour of five decades of the iconic Kenyan brand.

The Meru celebration was part of Kenya Cane’s year-long 50th anniversary campaign, “Spirit Yetu Idumu”, which recognises the people, culture and shared experiences behind the brand’s journey since 1976.

Speaking after the event, Victor Adada, Senior Brand Manager, Kenya Cane, said, “Meru gave us a wonderful reminder of what this 50-year milestone is about: people coming together, celebrating their culture and creating memories. Seeing different generations enjoy the music and share in the occasion made the celebration especially meaningful. As we mark 50 years, we are grateful to everyone who has been part of the Kenya Cane story, and we look forward to the next chapter with the same Kenyan spirit.”
As the anniversary celebrations continue across the country, Kenya Cane remains focused on honouring its heritage while embracing new experiences and opportunities to connect with Kenyans.
The Meru stop added another memorable chapter to the brand’s golden anniversary celebrations, with the spirit of “Spirit Yetu Idumu” ringing loud at Checkmate.

items.title: Black Friday: Your security doesn’t end at checkout
items.description: By Lynette Waweru, Cybersecurity Specialist at ESET East Africa One of the biggest sales tickets on the Jumia Kenya platform for 2026 is the smart TV alongside smartphones, mobile accessories and kettles.
content: By Lynette Waweru, Cybersecurity Specialist at ESET East Africa

One of the biggest sales tickets on the Jumia Kenya platform for 2026 is the smart TV alongside smartphones, mobile accessories and kettles. And it is the purchasing of these big ticket items that usually comes with warnings of scams and phishing and fraudsters every Black Friday. Criminals use trust to break into systems, lure shoppers away from real sites and create fake purchases. However, there is another security threat that Kenyan shoppers need to be wary of – what happens after you’ve bought the TV. A smart TV runs an operating system, connects to a home network and stores streaming logins, and this means it needs the same security awareness as your mobile device or laptop.

There is a good reason for this wariness. The National KE-CIRT/CC cybersecurity report for July to September 2026 names Android TVs as among the top targets of mobile application attacks, together with Android phones, set-top boxes and the Google TV app. The report recorded 177,732 mobile application attacks, and 27,4535,527 web application attacks, over the last quarter. Attackers misused the Android Debug Bridge, a developer feature that should be switched off on consumer devices, and exploited default credentials that had been left unchanged.

After the money has been spent on a top of the range smart TV, or home networking system, it is critical to spend time ensuring that it doesn’t become a gateway into your home and systems. In November, Google revealed that it had disrupted a botnet of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes, and attributed this backdoor to the manufacturer that had been licensed to shop Android TV devices with Google apps. According to reports, the manufacturer had embedded the malware in the firmware during manufacturing. While this specific incident involves set-top boxes, it shows that the security of a device balances on trust in the manufacturer, as well as the retailer, and the brand. And this trust can be misplaced at any point along the value chain.

The solution? Shoppers need to ask more questions about their products before they purchase them, regardless of the discounts or the size. It may be a beautiful TV, but if it doesn’t receive regular security updates or come from a trusted source, then it will be the start of a toxic relationship. Before you spend the money, get the full model number of the TV and look for the manufacturer’s written security update commitment for that model and find out how long security fixes are guaranteed for. The warranty and security updates are two separate considerations, and you need to know how long the company will support the security of your TV and how you can ensure it remains secured for the foreseeable.

The second check is when you set up the device. During setup, replace any changeable default device or administrator passwords – unchanged passwords are a significant weakness – and when you first connect to the Wi-Fi check for, and install, system updates before adding streaming apps. It’s worth enabling automatic updates if the model supports these and disable the Android Debug Bridge for now. Only install apps from trusted sources and check the app permissions – on a smart TV that means leaving the developer options switched off, downloading apps from the official store for the TV’s platform, and declining permissions an app does not need to do its job.

Retailers should also show the minimum security support date for a connected device alongside its price and warranty. It shows consumers that there are security options built-in and also provides a better benchmark when choosing between different models. If one is more protected than another, it is a genuine value-add on purchase. However, until retailers make this standard practice, the responsibility sits with the buyer who should ask for the security date before paying and spend time setting up their system with robust passwords, updates and permissions. A smart TV bought this Black Friday may stay on the home network for many years, and the decisions made now will impact how well it stays protected and how much risk it introduces to the home.
